newsitem.title: CHINA: Beijing slams West as using Tibet to split China.
newsitem.headline: Beijing slams West as using Tibet to split China.

text.p: Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen blasted Western media on Wednesday for using Tibet as a tool to split China, and praised the restive region for its role in defending the integrity of the motherland.

Western media reports saying Tibetan culture had suffered under Beijing's rule were groundless, Xinhua news agency quoted Qian as telling a meeting of deputies from the Himalayan region attending the annual session of the National People's Congress, or parliament.
"The attacks and slanders hurled by the Western media are completely groundless," Qian said without identifying which reports he found to be erroneous.
Beijing has come under fire from rights groups and Western governments for its heavy-handed treatment of those seeking autonomy or independence for Tibet.
China dismisses such criticisms as interference in its internal affairs.
Qian took a swipe at the Buddhist region's exiled god-king, the Dalai Lama, saying the spiritual leader was being used by foreign forces seeking to split China.
"International anti-China forces often used the Tibet issue and Dalai Lama as their tools," Qian told the members of parliament.
The Dalai Lama, who fled his homeland in 1959 after an abortive uprising against Chinese rule, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his non-violent campaign for more autonomy for Tibet.
Qian praised the mountainous region -- which borders India, Nepal, Bhutan and Burma -- for playing an important strategic role in preserving China's territorial integrity.
"Tibet, as an important frontier defence in the southwestern part of our country, has a significant role in the struggle of safeguarding the motherland and opposing separatism," he said.
Deeply religious Tibet has been rocked in recent years by sporadic, sometimes violent, anti-Chinese unrest, with monks and nuns often at the forefront of demonstrations for independence.
Authorities tightened security and launched a manhunt across Tibet after a bomb exploded on Christmas Day outside government offices in the capital of Lhasa.
